title: Designing a ride-hailing service like Uber

facts.text: Customers see nearby cabs with ETA and pricing, book a cab and see the driver's location; drivers accept or deny rides, see the pickup location and mark the trip complete on reaching the destination.
The system needs high availability with minimal latency and scalability; extended requirements are trip ratings, payment processing, and metrics and analytics.
Assuming 100 million daily active users, 1 million drivers and 10 million rides daily, with 10 actions per user, the platform handles 1 billion requests daily, or 12K requests per second.
At 400 bytes per message, storage is about 400 GB a day and about 1.4 PB over 10 years, with a minimum ingress bandwidth of around 5 MB per second.

Tables hold customers, drivers, trips (source, destination, status), cabs (registration number, type), ratings and payments by trip ID; each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra.

Request a ride takes a customer ID, source and destination; cancel takes a customer ID and optional reason; accept or deny takes a driver and ride ID; start or end uses a driver and trip ID; rating takes a score.

Microservices own their data: customer, driver, ride (ride matching and quadtree aggregation), trip, payment, notification and analytics services, communicating over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

A customer requests a ride with source, destination, cab type and payment method; the ride service finds nearby drivers and the ETA and broadcasts the request; once a driver accepts, the customer sees the driver's live location and ETA.

Pulling location by periodic HTTP requests or long polling does not scale: it adds request overhead and most responses are empty; a WebSocket push model delivers data without delay and is full-duplex, unlike unidirectional Server-Sent Events.

A radius query on PostgreSQL or MySQL is too slow at scale; geohash encodes coordinates as hierarchical base-32 strings, so the customer's geohash is compared with drivers' geohashes, indexed in memory.

A quadtree, whose internal nodes have four children, splits two-dimensional space to search points in a range efficiently; split a node only past a threshold, update it on each driver location update, and cache the latest updates in Redis.
Race conditions arise when many customers request rides at once, so the ride matching logic is wrapped in a mutex and every action is transactional.

Nearby drivers are ranked by parameters such as average rating, relevance and past feedback so the best are notified first; under high demand, surge pricing temporarily raises prices in reaction to increased demand and limited supply.
Payments go to a third-party processor such as Stripe or PayPal, with a webhook capturing payment data; push notifications flow through a message queue or broker such as Kafka to FCM or APNS.

Shard by region, such as zip codes, with consistent hashing against uneven load; cache recent customer and driver locations in Redis or Memcached with LRU eviction, refilling from the database on a miss.

Remove single points of failure with multiple service instances, load balancers between clients, servers, databases and caches, read replicas and replicated caches; a dedicated broker such as Kafka or NATS makes notifications robust.

title: Proximity service

definition.text: A service that returns the places within a given radius of a location, such as nearby restaurants.

facts.text: A proximity design has two key services: a business service that adds, deletes and updates place information and lets customers view details, and a location-based service that returns the places near a given location and radius.
Storing each place's latitude and longitude and computing the distance to every place makes the query very inefficient.

The geohash algorithm speeds it up: divide the planet into four quadrants along the prime meridian and equator, keep dividing each grid into four, and name a grid by alternating longitude and latitude bits.
Nearby places in a grid are then found with a prefix match on the geohash column, for example geohash LIKE '01%'.
Geohash has limits: one grid can hold very many places (downtown New York) and another none (the ocean), so more complicated algorithms optimize the process.

title: Uber's technology stack

definition.text: The frameworks, protocols, databases and data tools behind Uber's apps and services.

facts.text: The web frontend uses Fusion.js, a React framework Uber built, and visualization.js for geospatial visualization; mobile apps use the RIB architecture with VIPER instead of MVC, in Swift for iOS and Java for Android.
Uber Gateway is a dynamic configuration on top of NGINX; client-server communication uses gRPC and QUIC, and APIs are defined with Apache Thrift.

Backend services use Spring Boot for Java, uAct for event-driven architecture and Cadence for asynchronous workflow orchestration; Flipr (later UCDP) is a unified configuration store and H3 a location-index store library.
The main OLTP store is the strongly consistent DocStore, which employs MySQL and PostgreSQL with the RocksDB engine.

Big data uses the Hadoop family with Hudi and Parquet file formats and Alluxio as cache; time-series data is in Pinot and AresDB; Hive, Spark and Marmaray process data, and Kafka and Flink handle messaging and streaming.
DevOps uses a monorepo with devpod environments and Spinnaker for continuous delivery, with uMetric for metrics, uMonitor for alarms and M3 as the observability database.

title: Dynamic pricing

definition.text: A pricing strategy, also called surge pricing, in which flexible prices are set from current market demand, rising at peak demand and falling at low demand.

facts.text: Raising prices at peak demand and lowering them at low demand encourages buying when demand is low and discourages it when demand is high; in some sectors economists see it as a more efficient allocation of limited resources.

Algorithmic pricing sets prices automatically to maximize the seller's profit, using data such as statistics on potential buyers, competitors' prices, the active buyer's personal information and the seller's own stock and sales targets.

Time-based pricing, common among online retailers, changes prices with the time of day; other methods price by cost plus a fixed profit, by competitors' prices, or by the value or elasticity of the product to buyers.

It is often criticized as price gouging, so operators add guardrails: Uber has capped how high surge pricing can go in emergencies since 2015, and drivers may hold off accepting rides until surge raises fares.

title: Nearest neighbor search

definition.text: The optimization problem of finding the point in a given set that is closest, or most similar, to a given query point.

facts.text: Closeness is a dissimilarity function, most often a distance metric such as Euclidean or Manhattan distance over a d-dimensional vector space; k-nearest neighbor search returns the k closest points instead of one.
It underlies databases, recommendation systems and vector databases, where nearest-neighbor lookup over embeddings retrieves semantically similar records.

The simplest exact solution is linear search: compute the distance from the query to every point, keeping the best so far, in O(dN) time with no search structure to maintain; comparing squared distances skips the square root.

Space partitioning avoids scanning every point: a k-d tree repeatedly bisects the search space and queries walk root to leaf, with average O(log N) time for randomly distributed points; the R-tree supports inserts and deletes.

In high-dimensional Euclidean space no general-purpose exact solution has polynomial preprocessing and polylogarithmic search time, tree indexes stop helping because most nodes must be examined, and naive search can on average win.
Approximate search may return a point within c times the distance to the true nearest; it is often almost as good, and trades guaranteed answers for speed or memory savings.

Proximity graph methods such as HNSW are the current state of the art for approximate search: greedy search hops to the neighbor closest to the query until a local minimum. Locality-sensitive hashing instead puts close points in one bucket.

Compression and clustering also speed search: a compressed copy of the vectors in RAM prefilters candidates before exact distances are computed from disk, or the database is clustered and only the most promising clusters are retrieved.
